description:
Project: Astronaut Health Monitoring Software (Offline-First Web/Mobile App). Real-time metric tracking and alerts. Will end up as a completed portfolio project.

Looking for team members:

UI/UX Designer (dashboards, icons, presentation).

Analyst / Researcher (NASA datasets, metrics).

Software Developer to help with code
summary:
AstroHealth is an onboard health computer that helps astronauts monitor, evaluate and act on their own health during long-duration missions, when Earth is up to 20 minutes away.

It gathers vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, respiration, blood pressure, temperature), sleep, exercise, radiation dose and a 30-second daily self-check of mood, stress and fatigue. It evaluates them with the NEWS2 clinical score and each astronaut's personal baseline, so deviations are caught before values leave generic norms. Color coding then shows status at a glance. It also guides action: an interactive body map explains each organ, how spaceflight hazards affect it, how to measure it, and when to call the crew medical officer. Alerts open step-by-step protocols. Mission Control receives the same data with a realistic communication delay.

The whole system runs in the browser with no server or internet, as it would have to on the way to Mars. We also prototyped an optional face-photo check for fatigue and facial puffiness; in this version it returns prepared demo answers.

Astronauts are not doctors. AstroHealth turns raw numbers into clear, timely decisions.
details:
What it does

AstroHealth is a self-care health computer for long-duration crews, built around three steps: gather → evaluate → act.

  • Gather. Simulated wearable sensors stream heart rate, SpO₂, respiration rate, blood pressure, temperature and activity. Astronauts add sleep, exercise and a 30-second daily self-check covering mood, stress, fatigue, sleep quality and symptoms. The system also tracks cumulative radiation dose and cabin environment: CO₂, O₂ and pressure per module.
  • Evaluate. Every reading is scored two ways. The first is the NEWS2 clinical early-warning score. The second is a personal baseline: a z-score against the astronaut's own history, so a rising resting heart rate is flagged even while it is still within population norms. The results feed a 0–100 readiness index and a green/yellow/red status for six body systems: cardiovascular, respiratory, bone & muscle, behavioral/sleep, immune and radiation.
  • Act. An interactive body map shows each organ colored by live status. Tapping an organ explains its function, which of NASA's five spaceflight hazards (RIDGE) affect it, how to measure it in microgravity, the normal range, what to do, and clear "call the crew medical officer" thresholds. Alerts open 12 step-by-step protocols, for example hypoxia, tachycardia, CO₂ rise, solar flare, infection and fatigue. A Mission Control view receives the same data over a simulated 12-minute link with message queueing, showing why decisions must be made onboard.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts are not doctors, and on a Mars mission they cannot wait for Earth. AstroHealth catches problems early through personal baselines, explains them in plain language, and tells the crew exactly what to do next. That reduces dependence on ground support and supports crew autonomy, which deep-space exploration will require.

How it works and tools used

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Recharts for dynamic trend charts, Lucide icons.
  • 3D landing: three.js with custom GLSL shaders for Earth (day/night, clouds, atmosphere), the NASA 3D Resources ISS model, and Earth textures by Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0). Sound is synthesized with the Web Audio API.
  • Simulation and analytics: Python (vital-sign and environment simulator, NEWS2, baselines, alert engine, communication-link model). It is configured in YAML, so thresholds, protocols, crew and scenarios are editable without code. It is tested with pytest.
  • Offline by design: the Python engine runs in the browser through Pyodide (WebAssembly), so the app works with no server and no internet, as an onboard system must. A FastAPI server version is also available.
  • Hardware: none required. Any laptop or tablet browser works. Sensors are simulated and designed to be replaced by real wearables.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude Code as a coding assistant during development.

Creativity

  • The clickable body map turns medical data into something you can explore.
  • Personal baselines are used instead of one-size-fits-all limits.
  • A scenario console lets judges trigger a solar flare, depressurization or tachycardia and watch the whole chain from detection to protocol to Earth notification.
  • A prototype face-photo check estimates fatigue, eye bags and the "puffy face" caused by fluid shift. In this version it returns prepared demo answers. The planned version runs on-device so photos never leave the spacecraft.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay and offline operation.
  • Privacy. Photo analysis is voluntary and on-device.
  • Accessibility. Color is always paired with icons and text, the app supports keyboard navigation, and there is reduced-motion support.
  • Honesty about limits. Formulas are labeled as a prototype, not a medical device.
  • Mission environments. The configuration supports different crews, modules and link profiles.
